questiontext.text: How many children does each node of a ternary search tree (TST) have?

answer.text: Three: less-than, equal, and greater-than

feedback.text: Correct — hence "ternary": low, equal, high.

answer.text: Two: left and right

feedback.text: No — that is a binary search tree; a TST adds a middle (equal) child.

answer.text: One per alphabet character

feedback.text: No — that is a plain trie node; a TST stores one character with three pointers.

answer.text: A variable number labeled with substrings

feedback.text: No — that describes a radix tree, not a TST.

generalfeedback.text: Each TST node holds one character and three children: less-than, equal, and greater-than — combining BST-style branching with trie descent.

questiontext.text: In a TST, what happens when you follow the equal (middle) child?

answer.text: You advance to the next character of the search key

feedback.text: Correct — the middle/equal child descends one position into the key.

answer.text: You compare the same character against a larger value

feedback.text: No — the greater-than child, not the equal child, does that.

answer.text: You restart the search from the root

feedback.text: No — descent continues; it does not restart.

answer.text: You skip to the end of the key

feedback.text: No — the equal child advances by exactly one character.

generalfeedback.text: Taking the equal child means the current character matched, so you move to the next character of the key — that is the trie-descent part of a TST.

questiontext.text: Compared with a plain trie, a ternary search tree is generally...

answer.text: More space-efficient — no full array/map of children per node

feedback.text: Correct — three pointers per node instead of one slot per alphabet symbol.

answer.text: Less space-efficient because of the extra middle child

feedback.text: No — three pointers beat a full per-node child array; TSTs use less space.

answer.text: Identical in memory, differing only in speed

feedback.text: No — the memory profiles differ; TSTs avoid the trie's wide child arrays.

answer.text: Unable to store variable-length strings

feedback.text: No — TSTs store variable-length string keys just fine.

generalfeedback.text: A plain trie may reserve a child slot per alphabet symbol at every node; a TST keeps just three pointers per node, so it is more space-efficient.

questiontext.text: Which capability do ternary search trees support well, like tries?

answer.text: Prefix / autocomplete and nearest-neighbour queries

feedback.text: Correct — TSTs support prefix, autocomplete, and near-match lookups.

answer.text: Constant-time hashing of the whole key

feedback.text: No — that is a hash table; a TST walks the key character by character.

answer.text: Range-sum queries over numeric arrays

feedback.text: No — that is a Fenwick/segment tree, not a TST.

answer.text: Maintaining a min-heap of priorities

feedback.text: No — heaps do that, not TSTs.

generalfeedback.text: Because it descends by character like a trie, a TST supports prefix queries, autocomplete, and nearest-neighbour (near-match) searches.

questiontext.text: In a ternary search tree, following the middle (equal) child advances the search to the next character of the key.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the equal child is the trie-descent step.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — the middle child does advance to the next character.

questiontext.text: A ternary search tree is just an ordinary binary search tree with no trie-like behaviour.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — a TST combines BST-style low/high branching with trie descent through the equal child.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — the equal child gives it trie-style character-by-character descent.

questiontext.text: In a TST, the middle child that is taken when the current character matches is called the ______ child (one word).

answer.text: equal

feedback.text: Correct — the matching path is the equal (middle) child.

answer.text: equal*

feedback.text: Correct — the matching path is the equal (middle) child.

questiontext.text: Which statements about ternary search trees are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Each node stores one character and has three children (low, equal, high)

feedback.text: Yes — that is the TST node structure.

answer.text: They are more space-efficient than a plain trie

feedback.text: Yes — three pointers instead of a full child array per node.

answer.text: Each node holds a full array of children, one per alphabet symbol

feedback.text: No — that is a plain trie; a TST keeps only three pointers.

answer.text: They cannot support prefix or autocomplete queries

feedback.text: No — TSTs support prefix, autocomplete, and nearest-neighbour queries.

generalfeedback.text: A TST stores one character per node with low/equal/high children, is more space-efficient than a plain trie, and supports prefix, autocomplete, and near-match queries with lookups around O(L + log n).
